research_text:
## Research brief

### 1. `SSLContext` scope and the reported `KeyManager[]` finding

`javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` represents a secure-socket protocol implementation and acts as a factory for secure socket factories and `SSLEngine` instances. It is initialized with an optional set of key managers, trust managers, and a secure-random source. Its documented initialization event is:

```java
SSLContext.init(KeyManager[] km, TrustManager[] tm, SecureRandom random)
```

The documented role of `km` is “sources of authentication keys”; `tm` supplies peer-authentication trust decisions. Either manager-array parameter may be `null`, in which case installed providers are searched for the highest-priority implementation of the appropriate factory; `random` may also be `null`, in which case a default implementation is used. Only the first manager of any particular implementation type in each supplied array is used. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

Accordingly, the detector message refers to the **first argument value of a call to `SSLContext.init`**—the `KeyManager[]` value—not to a TLS wire message, negotiated protocol, persisted format, or an `SSLEngine` event.

The official `KeyManagerFactory` API defines the documented factory route: it is a factory for key managers based on key material, its `init` accepts a `KeyStore` or provider-specific parameters, and `getKeyManagers()` returns the resulting `KeyManager[]`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/KeyManagerFactory.html))

The supplied CrySL `SSLContext` rule does **not** literally name `KeyManagerFactory`. Instead, it requires the analysis predicate:

```text
generatedKeyManagers[km];
```

The repository’s separate `KeyManagerFactory` CrySL rule declares that `getKeyManagers()` ensures precisely `generatedKeyManagers[keyManager]`. Thus, the detector wording “not observed coming from a KeyManagerFactory” is consistent with the cross-rule provenance predicate, rather than a statement made by the JDK `SSLContext` API documentation. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

### 2. Officially documented usage and remediation guidance

The official Java API documents these relevant usage semantics:

* Obtain an `SSLContext` using `SSLContext.getInstance(protocol)` or a provider-specific overload. The requested protocol is a standard protocol name; provider availability determines whether the call succeeds. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
* Initialize the context with `init(KeyManager[], TrustManager[], SecureRandom)` before using context operations that require initialization, such as creating socket factories or `SSLEngine` instances. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))
* A factory-produced array is a documented way to supply managers: initialize `KeyManagerFactory`, then obtain a `KeyManager[]` via `getKeyManagers()`; equivalently, initialize `TrustManagerFactory`, then obtain a `TrustManager[]` via `getTrustManagers()`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/KeyManagerFactory.html))
* Passing `null` for `km` or `tm` is explicitly API-valid and invokes provider selection of the appropriate factory. Passing `null` for `random` is also explicitly API-valid. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

**Limit of the official documentation:** the JDK documentation does **not** state that every non-factory-created `KeyManager[]` is incorrect or unsafe, nor does it prescribe a remediation specifically for a static-analysis finding about manager provenance. It documents the factory route and the provider-default (`null`) route as valid API behaviors. The requirement that a supplied non-null array be analysis-proven to originate from `KeyManagerFactory.getKeyManagers()` is a CrySL rule requirement, not an explicit JDK API requirement. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

The same distinction applies to trust managers: the JDK API documents trust-manager factories and null/default selection, while the CrySL rule adds a separate provenance requirement for `TrustManager[]`. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

### 3. Compatibility, formats, protocol support, and migration documentation

**Persisted formats.** The examined `SSLContext`, `KeyManagerFactory`, and `TrustManagerFactory` API documentation does not define a persisted or serialized format for an `SSLContext` or for changing the origin of the `KeyManager[]` supplied to `SSLContext.init`. No API migration path for such a format is documented in these sources. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

**Wire formats and negotiated protocol.** The API documentation distinguishes the `SSLContext` protocol-name request from per-connection settings. `SSLParameters` holds the protocols allowed for an SSL/TLS/DTLS connection and can be applied to `SSLSocket`, `SSLServerSocket`, or `SSLEngine`. `SSLEngine` documentation describes handshake negotiation, including agreement on a mutually available cipher suite. The sources reviewed do not state that replacing a supplied `KeyManager[]` with a factory-produced array changes a TLS wire format. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLParameters.html))

In particular, `SSLContext.getProtocol()` returns the name passed to `getInstance`; that fact alone is not documentation of the enabled protocol set or negotiated protocol version. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

**Platform-version support.** The Java SE 25 API requires every Java-platform implementation to support `TLSv1.2` and `TLSv1.3`. By contrast, the Java SE 11 API’s required list is `TLSv1`, `TLSv1.1`, and `TLSv1.2`, and the Java SE 8 API’s required list is only `TLSv1`. The historical specification lists therefore do not establish that `TLSv1.3` is universally available on every older implementation; `getInstance` is documented to throw `NoSuchAlgorithmException` if no provider supports the requested protocol. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

**Documented migration path.** No source reviewed provides a dedicated migration procedure for changing `SSLContext.init` manager provenance. The relevant documented compatibility boundary is provider support: both the protocol requested through `getInstance` and the selected factory implementation depend on available security providers. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html))

### 4. Exact matching rule in `SSLContext.crysl`

The primary CrySL source declares its governed specification type as:

```text
SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext
```

Its matching and forbidden-event clauses are, verbatim:

```text
FORBIDDEN
	getDefault() => Get;

EVENTS
	g1: getInstance(protocol);
	g2: getInstance(protocol, _);
	Get := g1 | g2;

	i1: init(km, tm, random);
	Init := i1;

	se1: eng = createSSLEngine();
	se2: eng = createSSLEngine(_,_);
	Engine := se1 | se2;
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

The source therefore states the following:

| Rule element | Governed receiver/type stated by source | Method and parameter-list constraint |
|---|---|---|
| Specification scope | `javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` | `SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` |
| Forbidden event | The specification’s `SSLContext` scope | `getDefault()` — zero arguments; it is forbidden and mapped to `Get` |
| `Get` | The specification’s `SSLContext` scope | `getInstance(protocol)` or `getInstance(protocol, _)` — one or two arguments; the second argument is represented by `_` |
| `Init` | The specification’s `SSLContext` scope | `init(km, tm, random)` — three arguments. The declared object types are `KeyManager[]`, `TrustManager[]`, and `SecureRandom`, respectively. |
| `Engine` | The specification’s `SSLContext` scope | `eng = createSSLEngine()` or `eng = createSSLEngine(_,_)` — zero or two arguments. |

The source then specifies this order, value constraint, and required predicates:

```text
ORDER
	Get, Init, Engine?
CONSTRAINTS
	protocol in {"TLSv1.2", "TLSv1.3"};

REQUIRES
	generatedKeyManagers[km];
	generatedTrustManagers[tm];
	randomized[random];
```

([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

For the reported message specifically, the condition evaluated is:

```text
generatedKeyManagers[km];
```

That condition is applied to the `km` argument captured by `init(km, tm, random)`. The rule also restricts the captured `protocol` value to exactly `TLSv1.2` or `TLSv1.3`; it does not contain an event for `SSLParameters.setProtocols`, `SSLSocket.setEnabledProtocols`, a TLS handshake, or negotiation. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

**Can it match a method that merely shares an API method name?** **No, not according to the type scope expressed in this source.** The source scopes the rule with `SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`; it does not declare any other receiver type or a name-only wildcard. However, the raw `.crysl` file does not itself include prose specifying the analysis engine’s method-resolution implementation. Therefore, the source establishes the intended governed API type, but this research pass cannot independently establish detector-specific dispatch-resolution behavior beyond that declared scope. ([raw.githubusercontent.com](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl))

## Source limitations and unresolved points

* The raw CrySL source establishes rule text and predicate names, but does not define the detector UI label `UnsatisfiedConstraint`, any possible `unknown` classification, or the exact data-flow implementation used by a particular CogniCrypt release.
* The supplied SHA-256 value was not independently recomputed in this research pass, and the cited raw GitHub `refs/heads/master` URL is branch-based rather than an immutable commit URL.
* The official JDK API sources document legal API semantics, not the application’s intended certificate-selection, trust, hostname-verification, provider, deployment, or peer-compatibility policy.
* No official source reviewed documents a persisted-format, wire-format, or explicit code-migration requirement associated solely with changing how the `KeyManager[]` value is obtained.
